justice: The complete absence of paved sidewalks and curb ramps severely limits accessibility for wheelchair users and older adults.
Space distribution is highly inequitable, with multiple wide asphalt lanes dedicated solely to motor vehicles and no space for active transport.
The lack of tactile paving along the roadside reduces fairness and navigability for visually impaired users.
safety: The absence of separated bike lanes and sidewalks forces cyclists and pedestrians into the vehicular roadway, increasing collision risks.
Clear double yellow lines and dashed white lane markings provide good lane guidance and safety specifically for drivers.
Tall streetlights ensure visibility for nighttime driving, but the environment lacks pedestrian-scale lighting for socially vulnerable groups.
livability: The complete lack of commercial buildings or mixed-use developments makes the street devoid of community vitality and destinations.
There are no benches, seating facilities, or gathering spaces along the grassy verge to support the leisure needs of older adults and adolescents.
The expansive vehicular lanes prioritize car throughput over human-centric social interaction, fundamentally diminishing livability.
sustainability: Extensive grassy verges, roadside shrubs, and newly planted trees provide permeable surfaces and basic green infrastructure.
The street design entirely lacks bus stops or public transit infrastructure, discouraging low-carbon travel options.
Wide expanses of black asphalt increase the urban heat island effect, and there are no visible integrated stormwater management features.
aesthetics: The uniform alignment of white streetlights and recently planted trees creates a neat, orderly visual corridor.
The asphalt street surface is exceptionally clean, well-maintained, and free of litter or debris.
The lack of visual diversity, street art, or engaging architectural facades makes the environment visually monotonous for active users.
comfort: The lack of benches or seating areas severely impacts physical comfort, especially for elderly pedestrians who require resting points.
Young roadside trees with sparse foliage provide insufficient canopy cover, leading to poor thermal comfort and high sun exposure.
The vast, exposed multi-lane road environment lacks human-scale protective elements, reducing psychological comfort for vulnerable road users.
walkability: The total absence of dedicated paved sidewalks forces pedestrians to walk on the uneven grassy verge or dangerously in the vehicular lanes.
No painted crosswalks, pedestrian refuges, or crossing signals are visible, severely hindering safe road navigation.
The lack of pedestrian-oriented destinations, shade, or street-level activity makes walking highly unattractive and impractical for all social groups.
bikeability: There are no dedicated or protected bike lanes on the asphalt, forcing cyclists to share space with fast-moving motor vehicles.
The lack of bicycle parking facilities, bike boxes, or cycling-specific signage makes the route unaccommodating for daily cycling.
The wide, multi-lane vehicular design naturally encourages higher vehicle speeds, creating an intimidating and unsafe environment for adolescent and elderly cyclists.
